repository.title: Power Analysis Discovery Lab
repository.description: Choose power-system tools by task: trace energy balances, compare dispatch constraints & plan reproducible grid studies.
repository.summary: A forked directory of power-flow, production-cost, microgrid, solver, and data resources. A simple daily balance helps distinguish an energy screen from a network or optimization study.
repository.audience: Power-system learners and engineers selecting a solver, dataset, or modeling framework.

model.equation: solar = S · max(0, sin(π(t−6)/12)); demand = D · (0.8 + 0.18 cos(2π(t−19)/24) + 0.12 exp(−((t−19)/3)²)); import = max(demand−solar−battery, 0).
assumptions: An idealized clear-day profile represents one 24-hour period.
Battery discharge is a fixed external power contribution; energy inventory and charge scheduling are omitted.
Solar share is capped at 100%; exports are not credited; grid carbon intensity is constant.
This fork preserves the anderson-optimization/awesome-power-analysis resource list.
The diagram has no buses, voltage angles, reactive-power equations, line limits, or optimization objective.
Constant battery discharge is an external assumption; it cannot establish day-long energy adequacy.
model.introduction: Use a one-bus balance to decide what additional method the engineering question needs. No listed power-flow solver, market model, dataset, or network is executed by this page.

modules.title: Distinguish power from energy
modules.objective: Read an instantaneous power balance and identify which additional time information energy accounting needs.
steps: Review the Power Flow, Production Cost Modeling, and Microgrid sections.
Apply 500 kW demand baseline, 600 kW PV peak, and zero battery contribution.
Inspect noon and evening; explain why a kW value is not a daily kWh total.
modules.reflection: Which data and equations would a power-flow study need that this single-bus screen omits?

modules.title: Identify the missing inventory constraint
modules.objective: Explain how a fixed battery power contribution differs from a storage schedule.
steps: Retain the same demand and PV profile.
Add 100 kW battery discharge and predict the evening import reduction.
Calculate the energy that six hours of this contribution would require, then find a storage-capable tool category in the list.
modules.reflection: Why is lower grid import insufficient evidence that a battery dispatch is feasible?

modules.title: Choose a method for the stress case
modules.objective: Separate demand adequacy, network feasibility, and economic optimization.
steps: Increase baseline demand to 800 kW while reducing PV peak to 400 kW.
Keep the illustrative 100 kW battery contribution and inspect the 19:00 shortfall supplied by the grid.
Map three questions—line overload, cheapest dispatch, and energy availability—to the directory categories.
modules.reflection: Which result would require AC network data, and which could be explored in a single-bus planning model?

modules.title: Write a tool-and-data study plan
modules.objective: State a bounded study question with explicit source, units, and validation requirements.
steps: Use 500 kW baseline demand, 300 kW PV, and no battery contribution.
Compare the noon and evening balance before proposing a solver.
Read the local contribution guidance and draft a shortlist containing model class, data needs, license, and a reproducible test case.
modules.reflection: What would distinguish a transparent screening result from an approved operational dispatch?
